The Challenge

The Exhibit House,
Exhibiting.

EXHIBITOR Show is the one trade show built specifically for the people who build trade shows: exhibit and event marketing managers who evaluate companies like Czarnowski for a living. Every prospect, client, and competitor walking that floor already knew what a good booth looked like. An eye-catching structure wasn't a differentiator there. It was table stakes.

Czarnowski needed to prove, in front of the toughest audience in the industry, that it could think the way it asked its own clients to think. It needed to do that again the following year, and the year after that, without the idea going stale or the budget scrutiny (real, in an economy still climbing out of 2008 and 2009) catching up with it.

About the Show

One Exhibitor.
Three Creative Booth Designs.

EXHIBITOR Show gathers exhibit and event marketing decision-makers each spring for education sessions and a floor full of exhibit houses competing for the same clients. Standing out here means standing out to people whose job is knowing better.

“The word ‘jump’ was a simple, accessible metaphor that would suggest how extraordinary marketers hurdle over obstacles and bound past conventional restraints.”

From “Quantum Leap,” Exhibitor Magazine's case study on the campaign

Year One earned its own trade-press feature: a full case study in EXHIBITOR Magazine's December 2011 issue, crediting the campaign with beating both its qualified-lead and new-prospect-meeting goals by 50 percent. “We wanted to pay tribute to the exhibit and event managers out there who see a little further, and in doing so attract those who aspired to be all-star marketers,” Czarnowski's director of marketing, Janine Makar, told the magazine.

Chapter One  /  2011

JuMP!

The finished 20′×30′ Czarnowski booth at EXHIBITOR2011. Three sculptural steel rings, 12 feet tall and 16 feet across, hung over a center stage rigged with 30 high-speed cameras.

The idea started as a single word. Czarnowski's marketing team debated images, catchphrases, and slogans before landing on “jump,” a metaphor simple enough to hang an entire year of programming on: jump for joy, jump at the chance, jump the curve. Anyone who broke away from the middle of the bell curve to lead their industry became a “Curve Jumper.”

One month out, Czarnowski shipped media kits, a branded tee, and a pair of red-and-white Chuck Taylors to seven writers and editors at three targeted trade titles, then followed with a three-part e-blast to roughly 1,000 registered attendees explaining the Curve Jumper concept and inviting them to jump the curve at the booth. On the floor, staff in JUMP tees and red Chucks opened with lines like “You look like a curve jumper,” then walked qualified visitors through an eLit touchscreen presentation, about 15 minutes each, built to show, not tell, how Czarnowski could move their program forward.

Every visitor, qualified or not, got invited to the center of the booth for the ring. Thirty high-speed cameras caught each jump from every angle and cut it into a personal highlight reel, delivered by email with a link to share on Facebook and Twitter. It was the one idea the rest of the year's programming pointed back to: don't just hear about jumping the curve, do it, on camera, in front of everyone.

The night before the show opened, 49 customers were treated to dinner at an upscale Asian restaurant, crashed by a ten-person professional flash mob dancing to the Pointer Sisters' “Jump (for My Love)” and Van Halen's “Jump.” The mob resurfaced 15 more times on and off the show floor before the week was out, each appearance texted ahead to a growing customer list. Everyone who attended left with the same kit staff wore all week: red Chucks, a JUMP tee and hat, and a copy of Creating Customer Evangelists, whose co-author Jackie Huba gave a 15-minute talk at the dinner.

Chapter Two  /  2012

Who is CJ?

Year two took the abstraction, the curve jumper, and gave it a face, or rather, hid its face on purpose. “CJ” became a recurring mystery figure: performers in full black bodysuits, stitched with the question “WHO IS CJ?” or “WHAT IS A CURVE JUMPER?”, worked the show floor and the booth in total anonymity, letting the campaign's own attendees supply the answer.

Before the show opened, CJ made appearances on stilts, inside a spinning circus ring, and mid-acrobatics, including a professional performer holding a one-handed handstand in Czarnowski's own “jump!” gear and red Chucks in the middle of a crowded aisle, planting the brand mid-flip in front of foot traffic that had nowhere else to look.

Inside the booth, that rotating red disc installation put the question directly to visitors: “What kind of CJ do you want to be?” The screens answered with a taxonomy of marketer personas, Trend Hunter, Influencer, Curve Jumper, Storyteller, turning a self-identification quiz into the booth's lead-qualifying mechanism. Three CJ silhouettes worked the floor continuously throughout the show.

The campaign peaked the Sunday before the show opened, at the VIP JUMP Party at China Grill: 100 people invited, 90 RSVPs, 68 confirmed guests plus 14 walk-ins, and 198 of them stepping up to jump for the photo booth before the night was out. Three targeted e-blasts, themed CJ, Powerhouse, and Formula, drove the invite list, with open rates as high as 42.6 percent.

Chapter Three  /  2013

Leave Your Mark

The third year traded spectacle for authorship. Instead of watching Czarnowski jump, or watching CJ jump, visitors were handed an LED light wand and asked to draw, in a single long exposure, whatever they wanted around themselves. Each result printed instantly as a Polaroid-style photo and got clipped to a growing gallery wall inside the booth, so every visitor's mark became part of the booth itself by the time the show closed.

It was a deliberate shift in the campaign's logic. Years one and two asked attendees to prove they belonged to a category, the Curve Jumper, then CJ. Year three didn't ask anything. It just handed over the pen and let three years of brand equity in “jump” do the rest of the work quietly, in the background, on a tagline that read simply: “We love what we do.”

The VIP party moved to Border Grill, Sunday, March 17, 6 to 9 p.m., running the same 100-guest format that had scored 1.25 out of 5, “Excellent,” the highest-rated element of the show, the year before. It anchored a project with the highest goals the campaign had set yet: prove a direct line to $1 million in new business within 18 months, engage 85 percent of booth visitors with an interactive element, and convert 50 highly qualified leads out of 200 badge scans across 175 unique companies.

My Role

Everything Outside
the Booth Walls.

The booth itself, design, fabrication, install, was Czarnowski's own craft on display. As project manager and vendor sourcer, my job was everything around it: the people, parties, print, and payables that turned three weeks on a trade show floor into a three-year brand story.

Guest List & RSVP Management

Owned the master invite and RSVP pipeline for all three VIP JUMP parties, cross-referencing show-floor check-in lists against RSVPs, tracking walk-ins in real time, and reporting attendance back to leadership after each event.

Vendor & Talent Sourcing

Sourced and coordinated every outside vendor beyond the booth structure itself: the ten-person flash-mob dance troupe, the acrobat and stilt performers who worked the CJ activations, the jump- and light-photography crews, and the custom framing vendor that turned show-floor photos into personalized client keepsakes.

Swag & Wearables

Ordered and tracked every branded giveaway across three years, red Chuck Taylors, JUMP tees and hats, pedometers, Starbucks cards, and copies of Creating Customer Evangelists, matching quantities to lead tiers so the best gifts reached the best leads.

Venue & Hospitality

Booked and managed the off-floor customer events each year, the 2011 launch dinner, China Grill in 2012, Border Grill in 2013, negotiating room, catering, and run-of-show with each venue.

Budget & Vendor Payables

Maintained and recorded the budget across every non-booth line item, suite activity, speaker-session logistics, party production, giveaways, photography, and framing, feeding real spend back into a total program budget that topped $274,000 by 2013.

Post-Show Follow-Through

Built the post-show machine after each party ended: the JUMP-party photo montage and survey, custom-framed client photos for personalized thank-yous, physical follow-up mailers to qualified leads, and the team survey that scored the program's own performance year over year.

What Made It Work

Looking Back

  • One word carried three different creative executions without ever feeling repeated: jump, then a persona built around jumping, then an activity that let guests jump for themselves.
  • Turning self-identification into the qualifying mechanic, Curve Jumper, then CJ, made lead-scoring feel like a game rather than a form.
  • Off-floor spend, dinners, flash mobs, framed photos, did as much brand work as the booth itself, and it's the part of a program most exhibit houses skip.
  • Team surveys scored the program honestly every year; lead-tracking devices and eLit stations came back as the weakest link two years running, and that data shaped where budget went next.
  • Vendor and logistics coordination scaled from a single dinner reservation in Year One to a fully budgeted, multi-vendor production by Year Three, without losing the informality that made the parties work.

Three years, three campaigns, one exhibit house proving, in front of the toughest audience in its industry, that it could out-market its own marketers.
